doc.title: David Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2022

title: Five voices as the sweet spot and how the octet began with Freddie Hubbard
summary: Weiss says five horns is his preferred size, recounting how a Freddie Hubbard record and demos for young writers led him to form his octet.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Wow. Well we’ve been at it for about an hour and it’s very fascinating. I wanted to get one question in. If you had a tune, let’s say you started it at the piano or something, and then you went for a walk and you start I don’t know if you do this or not but maybe you’re arranging it in your head thinking of the possibilities. What is the sweet spot for you as far as how many voices you have to work with?

Wow. Good question. I’m going to say five. That’s what I settled on. I mean I guess my patter about this has changed. There was a point where I could say look I never wrote a big band chart except for my final in college. You know? It never interested me in that way. I like small groups and I think the path I took and how — I settled on octet because, it was actually a Freddie Hubbard thing. Freddie was having his chop problems, he owed a record company a record. I was working with the producers and we were, you know, like ideas. I said well why don’t we put a slightly larger ensemble around him? Buffer, you know, he was a great composer, buffer the material and make it sound more full and then he just has to pick his spots, you know, which became the whole reason we did the thing. So we did that record and that’s the first time, and they threw me a couple of arrangements. I think Bob Belden did one or two and Bob Mintzer did a couple. And they threw me a couple. And that’s the first time I think I wrote for that size band and I liked it. And it inspired me to put together that octet. That, plus that same production company was young lions time and a French company didn’t have their finger on the pulse of what was going on in New York and paid us to make demos of all these young artists. And those guys, like gave it to me, because they didn’t want to be bothered. So I produced them all and when I walked away it was like wow, these guys can write. There’s nobody here, no innovators, there’s nobody here that’s like oh wow great solos. But the writing was great and that’s what I combined. I told those kids like hey I’m going to put together an octet and we’ll get together every week and just write. Write whatever you want, and that five was perfect. You can retain the small group thing. The material could have much more impact when you want it to have impact, you know, it just seemed like a nice — I mean I love sextet too and I guess the Cookers wound up to be somewhere in the middle because it needed to keep, to retain, when we originally did it it was Night of the Cookers. Night of the Cookers is two trumpets so we had to retain the two trumpets. And I think Night of the Cookers is two trumpets and alto and I wanted a little more — two trumpets and alto for an arranger, it’s a little top heavy let’s say.
